§7.3.4 Iconography and Symbols

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

text-iconography-and-symbols · text images marks

✅ Normative

An icon that carries meaning MUST NOT be dropped. It MUST be rendered as a bracketed semantic tag in the icon's position: one lower-case word naming what the icon means — [yes], [no], [locked] — with : degree where the icons are graded ([water: 3], [sun: partial]), and [icon: shape] naming the shape where the meaning is unclear ([icon: sun]). The vocabulary is open: the word is whatever names the meaning on this page.

Small symbols and images that stand in for a value rather than decorate — a tick in a feature-comparison column, a padlock, a sun or water icon used as the cell content itself.

Rendering

The icon is read the way the page intends it, and that reading is written in brackets:

| Feature | Basic     | Pro   |
| SSO     | [locked]  | [yes] |
  • Each icon MUST produce one tag, in the position the icon occupies.
  • Where an icon has no clear meaning in context, the tag MUST describe what is drawn — [icon: sun] — rather than guess a value.
  • Where the icons are graded, the tag MUST carry the degree, not just the presence: [sun: full] / [sun: partial], [water: 3] / [water: 1]. A tag that distinguishes the values beats a prettier glyph that does not.

Why a tag, and an open vocabulary

A tag reads back unambiguously and does not depend on a glyph existing, where the nearest Unicode character or emoji may not exist or may carry a different meaning. Its word is not drawn from a fixed list: no list would cover every icon, so the word is whatever names the meaning on this page, in lower case, used the same way throughout the document.

Why it matters

When the icon is the value, dropping it empties the table. A feature matrix or a scorecard whose marks are gone says nothing at all. This is the same failure as Color as the Value§9.6.4, where a coloured fill with no text becomes an empty cell and the table stops meaning anything.

❌ Counter-sample — graded icons flattened to one glyph

A plant-list table with two icon-valued columns — Sun and H₂O. The printed page on the left uses graded symbols: a filled, a half-filled or an empty sun, and one, two or three water droplets. The parse preview on the right renders both columns as a single ☀️ and a single 💧.

That is the failure this rule exists to prevent. The icons were not dropped — they were flattened. A plant needing three droplets and one needing a single droplet come out identical, so the column still looks populated while the information it carried is gone. The columns are the whole point of the table: Sun and H₂O are the two facts a reader consults it for. The expected Markdown reads the empty sun as [sun: none]; the red outlines around the two columns are highlighting added to the figure, not part of the page.

Non-conforming output

Larkspur 2' x 1' ☀️ 💧 Partial shade, two droplets…
Fernwort 1.5' x 1' ☀️ 💧 Shade only, three droplets…
Coastal Sage 3' x 2' ☀️ 💧 Drought tolerant…

Icons standing in for labels

An icon that clearly supplies a field's label — a pin before an address, a handset before a phone number — MUST be rendered as a bracketed semantic label beside its value: [address], [phone], [web]. The nearest word (Address:) MUST NOT be substituted: it is not printed. An icon whose function is unclear is described by its shape instead of guessed.

✅ Sample — icons standing in for labels

The footer prints a pin, a handset and a globe before the address, the phone number and the website — no words. The pictorial labels become [address], [phone] and [web] beside their values.

Expected Markdown · footer band

PAGE 1 [address] 7 Merevald Circle NW Suite 400 Harrowgate, BV 20036 [phone] 202-555-0180 [web] halvernwlc.example

Markdown source
**PAGE 1** [address] 7 Merevald Circle NW Suite 400 Harrowgate, BV 20036 [phone] 202-555-0180 [web] halvernwlc.example
